lesson.title: Low Latency Networking: Shaving Off the Milliseconds That Matter
lesson.summary: Low latency networking is the collection of design choices, protocols, and infrastructure decisions aimed at minimizing both latency and jitter together, for the applications that genuinely need fast and predictable delivery.
lesson.body:
Latency is the time a packet takes to travel from source to destination, and jitter is how much that latency varies from one packet to the next. Some applications barely notice either one: downloading a large file or sending an email works fine whether it takes 20 milliseconds or 200. Other applications depend on both being small and predictable, and low latency networking is the collection of design choices, protocols, and infrastructure decisions aimed specifically at minimizing those two things together, not just average delay, but its variability too.

Several concepts covered earlier in this chapter sequence are, in part, low latency techniques even though they were not framed that way at the time. Content delivery networks and edge computing both work by physically shortening the distance data has to travel, which directly reduces latency, since the underlying transmission itself takes time. SDN's centralized traffic engineering can route flows around congested paths that would otherwise add queuing delay. Beyond those, dedicated techniques exist purely to shave down latency and jitter: kernel bypass networking, where an application talks almost directly to the network interface card instead of going through a general purpose operating system's networking stack, avoids overhead that adds up when every microsecond counts. RDMA, remote direct memory access, lets one server read or write another server's memory directly over the network without involving the remote machine's CPU at all, cutting out a significant source of delay in high performance computing and some data center applications. Careful queue and buffer management also matters: oversized buffers can reduce packet loss but let a queue build up under load, quietly adding latency and jitter, a widely recognized problem sometimes called bufferbloat.

High frequency trading is the example that makes the stakes concrete. Firms trading on price differences between markets sometimes pay to physically co locate their servers inside, or as close as possible to, a stock exchange's own data center, and lease direct fiber or even microwave links between exchanges, because a price advantage that exists for a few microseconds can be gone before a trade routed the normal way even arrives. A few extra microseconds of latency, insignificant for almost every other kind of application, can be the entire difference between a profitable and a missed trade. A more everyday example is real time voice or video, or online multiplayer gaming, where it is often jitter, not just average latency, that people actually notice: audio that arrives at wildly inconsistent intervals sounds choppy even if its average delay is fine. Applications like these commonly use a jitter buffer, deliberately holding incoming data for a small, consistent extra delay so it can be played back smoothly, trading a little added latency for a lot less perceived jitter.

There is no single trick that produces low latency networking, it comes from combining physical proximity, efficient software paths, careful protocol choices, and deliberate tradeoffs between latency and reliability, chosen based on what a specific application actually needs. Recognizing when an application genuinely needs both low latency and low jitter, rather than just high average throughput, is usually the first step, since the techniques involved often add complexity or cost that is not worth paying for traffic that does not need it.
